strengths: Well-motivated and conceptually clean framework: PartCo addresses a well-known limitation in Generalized Category Discovery (GCD)—over-reliance on global [CLS] token representations—by deriving explicit part-level correspondence priors from foundation model patch tokens.

Training-only, zero-inference-overhead plug-and-play module: PartCo acts as an auxiliary supervision loss during training and does not alter the backbone architecture or inference latency, making it straightforward to integrate into various parametric and non-parametric GCD baselines (e.g., SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx).

Thorough and convincing empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates strong and consistent performance gains across fine-grained (SSB benchmark: CUB, Stanford Cars, FGVC-Aircraft, plus Oxford-Pet, Herbarium19) and generic datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100), across multiple foundation backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, and CLIP).

Comprehensive ablations and diagnostic analysis: The authors provide detailed investigations into the order of part granularity (1st, 2nd, 3rd order), projection dimension, loss balance parameters, comparison with ground-truth part annotations on CUB (Hungarian matching), foreground-only masking vs. explicit part correspondence, computational overhead, and unknown category estimation ($K$-estimation).
weaknesses: Manual heuristic for granularity order selection: The choice between 1st-order (recommended for fine-grained datasets) and 2nd-order (recommended for generic datasets) part-level correspondence is currently determined by the dataset category type rather than learned dynamically or automatically selected per dataset/class.

Dependency on offline preprocessing: The part-level correspondence label construction requires an offline two-step PCA and $k$-means pass over the dataset before training. While manageable (e.g., 5–30 minutes for smaller benchmarks), it scales with dataset size (up to 180 minutes on ImageNet-100) and decouples part discovery from end-to-end representation learning.

Reliance on foundation model patch feature quality: As evidenced in the failure case analysis (Section S4), if the foundation model struggles with intra-class appearance shifts (e.g., age, seasonal plumage, generic low-texture regions), the unsupervised part clustering can degrade and hinder global representation learning on those specific categories.

strengths: Well-motivated and effective design: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) often struggles with fine-grained distinctions due to an over-reliance on global ([CLS]) embeddings. PartCo systematically leverages dense patch-level features from vision foundation models to establish explicit part-level correspondence priors without requiring manual part annotations.

Plug-and-play with zero inference overhead: PartCo serves as an auxiliary training objective that seamlessly integrates into various existing parametric and non-parametric GCD pipelines (e.g., SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx), leaving the host model's test-time inference pipeline and latency completely untouched.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: The method is benchmarked across fine-grained datasets (SSB, Oxford-Pet, Herbarium19) and generic datasets (CIFAR10/100, ImageNet-100) using multiple foundation backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP). The empirical gains on fine-grained datasets are substantial (e.g., up to +9.8% on SimGCD and +8.2% on SPTNet).

Thorough ablations and diagnostic analyses: The paper provides extensive supporting experiments, including validation against ground-truth CUB part annotations (achieving 80.8% alignment), comparison against background masking baselines, analysis of part granularity orders (1st vs. 2nd vs. 3rd order), evaluation under estimated cluster numbers (K-estimation), and computational cost analysis.
weaknesses: Reliance on domain prior for label granularity: The framework switches between 1st-order and 2nd-order part label construction based on whether a dataset is considered fine-grained or generic. While justified empirically, requiring prior knowledge about dataset granularity slightly detracts from the open-world discovery premise.

Potential vulnerability to pseudo-label noise in unsupervised part loss: In Eq. (7), unsupervised part-level contrastive pairs rely on the model's predicted pseudo-labels. In early training epochs when pseudo-labels are unreliable, this could introduce noisy supervision, yet the paper lacks an explicit study or discussion on warmup schedules or noise-handling mechanisms for this term.

Diminishing returns on generic benchmarks: As shown in Table 2, accuracy improvements on generic datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100) are relatively minor (often < 1%), indicating that part correspondence priors primarily benefit fine-grained semantic shifts rather than coarse-grained categorization.

Lack of error bars / standard deviations: Tables 1 and 2 report single-run results without standard deviations across multiple random splits or seeds, which would strengthen the statistical rigor given the variance inherent to clustering and Hungarian matching.

strengths: Clear motivation and intuitive design: The paper addresses a known limitation of Generalized Category Discovery (GCD)—the over-reliance on global classification ([CLS]) tokens—by leveraging the spatial granularity inherent in patch tokens to capture part-level semantic correspondences across known and novel classes.

Broad empirical gains across benchmarks: PartCo provides consistent and notable performance improvements when integrated into diverse baseline architectures (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx) across both fine-grained datasets (CUB, Stanford Cars, FGVC-Aircraft, Oxford-Pet, Herbarium19) and generic datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100).

Inference efficiency: The method acts purely as a training-time supervisory objective. At inference time, the model retains the host baseline's original inference path and latency without adding architectural complexity or test-time compute overhead.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies: The submission provides thorough complementary evaluations in the appendix, including validation against ground-truth part annotations on CUB (Hungarian matching), evaluations under unknown cluster count estimation (K-estimation), robustness across different foundation models (DINOv2, DINOv3, and CLIP), and failure/success case analyses.
weaknesses: Heuristic selection between 1st- and 2nd-order part granularities: The choice between 1st-order part labels (for fine-grained datasets) and 2nd-order part labels (for generic datasets) is decided based on a manual prior regarding dataset granularity rather than being dynamically or adaptively inferred by the algorithm.

Sensitivity to initial PCA sampling and frozen backbone quality: The label construction relies on PCA fitted over a sampled subset of labeled images (one per known class). The paper lacks analysis on variance across different sampled subsets or sensitivity to the foreground threshold (tau_obj = 0.6). Furthermore, the quality of part correspondence is strongly dependent on the emergent spatial properties of the frozen foundation model.

Potential error propagation from pseudo-labels: The unsupervised part contrastive loss (Eq. 7) pairs patch features using predicted pseudo-labels. In early training epochs or under severe class ambiguity, inaccurate pseudo-labels could reinforce erroneous part-category associations, an effect that is not fully analyzed theoretically or empirically.
